article_title: Correlation of excellence in different school subjects based on a study of school grades.
citation: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Matched 32-pupil grade-record cohort from Urbana High School (1908-1912)
description: A dataset of school grades for 32 pupils, 18 girls and 14 boys, who entered Urbana High School in the fall of 1908 and graduated in the spring of 1912, studied the same subjects under the same instructors, and were selected after examining "the records of the pupils for the past six years." The authors tabulated ranks and grades in algebra, civics, American history, geometry, Latin and four years of English, dividing pupils into four equal groups of eight as the unit of comparison.
requirements: Pupils must have undergone the same treatment and lived under the same conditions, including identical instructors, subjects, and years of schooling, to give what the authors call a constant basis for trustworthy results.
constraints: The group is a single small cohort from one school; the authors repeatedly qualify conclusions with 'so far as this group is concerned' and 'with regard to the group studied.'
examples: The authors ranked pupils by algebra grades, divided them into four groups of eight, and checked whether a pupil in group I in algebra appeared in group I in civics and the other subjects.
key_sources: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Game-based e-learning is more effective than a conventional instructional method: a randomized controlled trial with third-year medical students.
citation: Boeker Martin, Andel Peter, Vach Werner, Frankenschmidt Alexander. (2013). Game-Based E-Learning Is More Effective than a Conventional Instructional Method: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Third-Year Medical Students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0082328
title: Uro-Island educational adventure game for phase contrast microscopic urinalysis
description: Uro-Island is an electronic adventure game developed at the University Medical Center Freiburg "built on the open source Wintermute game engine" for Windows computers. The player controls a character stranded on an island who explores scenarios, dialogues with non-player characters, gathers items, and masters quests covering "exactly the same urine pathologies as described in the script" in increasing difficulty, with the goal of reaching a diagnosis to regain freedom.
requirements: Learning contents must be integrated into the story in separate modules without destroying the game's nature, per the article's discussion of serious games
Development requires interdisciplinary teams of domain experts and game developers
constraints: No widely accepted guidelines exist on how to teach effectively with games or how to implement large quantities of educational material as gaming content
Game development remains work-intensive even with inexpensive frameworks
target_learners: third-year undergraduate medical students in urology
target_learning_goals: phase contrast microscopy of native urine: sampling, diagnostic methods, morphology of pathological components, and assignment of findings to urological diseases
examples: Students in the intervention arm trained on two PCs installed with the game, with no further written material, while the control group received three exemplars of an 8-page script
key_sources: Boeker Martin, Andel Peter, Vach Werner, Frankenschmidt Alexander. (2013). Game-Based E-Learning Is More Effective than a Conventional Instructional Method: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Third-Year Medical Students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0082328
